Subject: Please oppose unproven and potentially dangerous carbon capture projects -- Guidance: Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Sequestration (Document ID: CEQ-2022-0001-0001)

Dear Chair Brenda Mallory and members of the White House Council on Environmental Quality,

I’m deeply concerned about the viability of carbon capture, utilization, and sequestration ("CCUS"). CCUS is largely new and unproven technology, yet the federal government is preparing to spend billions of taxpayer dollars on this and other unproven climate schemes.

President Biden and members of his administration have regularly and correctly named climate change as an existential threat to humanity. But investing in CCUS is a dangerous distraction from real climate solutions. Capturing carbon dioxide is a very energy intensive process, and it allows for continued extraction and burning of coal, oil, and gas. These operations have poisoned communities for decades, and capturing emissions at the final step of energy production does nothing to prevent the negative air, water, and health impacts associated with drilling and mining.

Developing CCUS at a large scale would also require thousands of miles of new pipelines to transport liquefied carbon dioxide. These pipelines pose a grave threat to public safety, as vapor clouds of carbon dioxide can easily spread for miles and lead to hallucinations, intoxication, asphyxiation, and death.

It is possible to transition our economy to 100% clean, renewable energy through rapid electrification, phasing out fossil fuels, and improved land management and restoration, keeping global warming at or below 1.5 degrees Celsius without utilizing CCUS.

I urge you to set aside the distraction of carbon capture and instead mobilize the resources of the federal government to support a true clean, renewable energy revolution.

Thank you for your consideration of my comments. Please do NOT add my name to your mailing list. I will learn about future developments on this issue from other sources.

Sincerely,
Christopher Lish
San Rafael, CA

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality docket number CEQ-2022-0001

Our federal government should not be permitting any Carbon Capture and Sequestration activities.
Carbon Capture and Sequestration (CCS) technology should not be permitted plain and simple. CCS is just another attempt by the natural gas and coal industries to prolong their lifespan. CCS-equipped power plants end up burning more fuel to produce the same amount of electricity. And unlike already existing renewable forms of energy which produce minimal greenhouse gas emissions, CCS only reduces the greenhouse gas emissions of a gas or coal energy plant by about 40 percent In other words, if we wish to ensure the future of human civilization, CCS is not going to get us there.
On simple economic terms, currently, despite billions of dollars of both government support and industry investment, CCS technology is still incapable of competing with other energy sources. Meanwhile, large scale energy storage capacity for renewables is developing rapidly making the financing of CCS even less attractive.
Gas and coal fired power plants use large amounts of water, a resource that will be in increasingly short supply, and pollute the air with a variety of toxic materials including mercury, particulate matter, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Why on earth would we want to continue using these environmentally destructive methods to generate power?
Transportation and storage of carbon dioxide (CO2) comes with its own set of issues, since CO2 is denser than air and CO2 infrastructure is prone to leakage, and exposure to concentrations of CO2 higher than 10 percent can be fatal, communities who host this infrastructure will be put at real risk.
In other words, CCS is an expensive boondoggle whose primary purpose is to line the pockets of the fossil fuel industry.
If we are genuinely interested in decarbonizing our economy while creating good paying jobs for those who will be most affected by a green transition, we need to use a combination of natural sequestration methods along with a sharp reduction of our reliance on fossil fuels and fossil fuel based products.
Improved forest management as well as planting new forests, conserving and restoring peatlands and coastal wetlands, restorative agricultural practices such as no-till techniques, crop cover rotation, agroforestry, improved lifestock management, the restoration of seagrass meadows or growing kelp or shellfish all help to sequester carbon while, if done in a holistic manner, providing us with cleaner air, water, and increased biodiversity.
Rather than investing in CCS we should be installing solar panels and erecting wind turbines in an environmentally sensitive manner, as well as funding energy efficient retrofits of public and private buildings and reclaiming abandoned coal mines and orphaned oil and gas wells. If we focused on decreasing our energy use and replacing fossil fuels with renewable energy sources we would reap a far larger bang for the buck without the catastrophic side effect of handing a lifeline to the very fossil fuel companies who are destabilizing our climate, destroying wildlife habitat, and polluting our air and water.
Other policies which should be pursued, instead of CCS, if we wish to live in a better world, include radically reducing the amount of plastic we use and putting research dollars into discovering both alternatives to petrochemical based plastics and new methods for producing these alternatives that use renewable energy. The same policies should be followed for developing substitutes for cement and cement manufacturing. New approaches to steel manufacturing that rely on renewables are already being successfully developed. It is only our unwillingness to embrace real solutions to our climate crisis that make CCS attractive.
If, however, despite all these reason not to continue to invest in CCS technology, our government insists on permitting unproven CCS projects, then this same government should ensure that communities who are subjected to the presence of power plants that are outfitted with Carbon Capture devices, CO2 pipelines, or CO2 injection sites have access to the best possible health care and legal representation. They are going to need both.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number, CEQ-2022-0001

I understand that consistent with the Utilizing Significant Emissions with Innovative Technologies (USE IT) Act, the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) is seeking comment on an interim guidance document, “Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Sequestration Guidance,” to assist Federal agencies with the permitting and regulation of CCUS activities in the United States.

I recommend that we back up a step and look at the proper frame for CCUS and not rush into permitting and regulating.
•Federal funding needs to be small and R&D focused. It can’t be billions of dollars given to unproven technologies, which is what CCUS is at this stage. Consider: CCUS would be going strong around the world if the carbon could actually be captured and used commercially – without government subsidies.
•Federal funding needs to be aligned with efforts to reduce point sources of carbon. A technology that is an excuse for carbon-as-usual, e.g., business as usual, is not worthy of federal dollars.
oEnhanced oil recovery (EOR) is not a use consistent with carbon reduction goals. Rather, federal incentives would be better spent to reduce oil demand
oDAC at a thermal power plants is not consistent with carbon reduction goals. Rather, movement to low carbon power production is the solution.
oCCUS needs to be limited to hard-to-decarbonize industries such as cement.
oCCUS needs to be onsite at the carbon polluter.

Unless the carbon returns to a solid, we have not really “captured” it. (It’s a gas!) And, unless it is turned into a usable product, we are missing the “U” in CCUS. What would be appropriate CCUS? That is where R&D and imagination are needed. Small demonstration projects are what is needed at this point.
•Can carbon be captured as graphite with a commercial purpose? Say, in construction as a cement replacement?
•Can carbon be capture in plants with an end-use as a commercial product? Say, as a plastic replacement?

Inappropriate approaches to CCUS
•CCUS for electric power generation. There are lower-cost ways to decarbonize the power sector
•Building pipelines to CO2 sequestration sites. Pipeline construction damages the ecosystem and takes away property rights.
•Using existing pipelines. A gas is volatile. Gas escapes. Compressor stations vent. The federal government has no business throwing huge sums of money at archaic systems.

By staying small, the federal government can avoid a boondoggle of a federal program. The billions of dollars mentioned for CCUS infrastructure paint a picture of a huge bureaucracy struggling to define just what it is permitting (CDR? DAC? BECCS?); and how to coordinate with other agencies on pipelines, emissions, and environmental justice; and how to avoid the politics that accompany federal handouts.

By funding some meaningful R&D to turn CO2 into a nongaseous state, taxpayer dollars can be used conservatively and wisely.

Furthermore, there should be no use of the 45Q tax credit for imported CO2. A LNG exporter posited that empty tankers could drop off a load of LNG in Asia and return with a ship full of CO2. This is unacceptable.

Thank you.

I am specifically commenting on the use of carbon, capture, and storage (CCS) of CO2 produced by bioethanol plants and the use of pipelines to transport that CO2. (2) The CO2 captured by these projects is the relatively pure CO2 from the fermentation process and not the larger emissions from the use of natural gas or coal for the distillation of ethanol and the drying of dried distillers grains (DDG’s). https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/LCA_of_Corn_Ethanol_2018_Report.pdf. P.94

(3) “The impacts of climate change should be planned for and addressed in the design, construction, and maintenance of carbon dioxide pipelines.” [1]
The use of ethanol in gasoline is mandated by Federal law but the use of gasoline hopefully will diminish with increasing adaption of electric vehicles.
Currently, there are only 5,000 miles of existing CO2 lines, meaning there is little experience with a wide range of operational — and safety — issues likely to arise from such a massive new system. https://www.huffpost.com/entry/gassing-satartia-mississippi-co2-pipeline_n_60ddea9fe4b0ddef8b0ddc8f and https://www.dnv.com/oilgas/laboratories-test-sites/dense-phase-spadeadam-video.html and https://www.ecowatch.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/1553742266-origin.jpg

While I personally benefit from higher corn prices due to the market for ethanol, I object to my tax dollars being spent to perpetuate the production of ethanol from corn. I agree that CCS and CCUS will probably be needed for certain essential industries such as concrete and steel but their use for ethanol is not essential. The use of 45Q tax credits should not be used to extend the life of polluting industries such as those producing ethanol and those using the combustion of coal.

comment: Our company is capturing CO2 from large buildings where it is difficult to address lower emissions with other technologies.  We capture CO2 from operations of the buildings that rely on commercial boilers or on CHP systems. We have one fully operational system and will capture at least 3000 tons per year starting the fall of 2022 when 5 more systems will come online. Emissions from buildings account to 70% of emissions, on average, in cities, and most of the emissions come from large buildings that are currently a challenge to address via other means such as electrification.  Given that immediate emissions reductions are needed from all sectors, including buildings, we would like CEQ and DOE efforts to consider onsite carbon capture from buildings.  Our process allows us to build modular systems that capture and liquify the CO2 onsite.  We then partner with others to mineralize the CO2 in concrete or displace petroleum in green methanol production.  Given the large quantity of eligible building stock (large multi-family, commercial, hospitals, muni buildings, colleges)  as well as larger facilities relying on CHP, our volumes will quickly multiply to tens of thousands of tons per year in New York City alone, leading to a need for sequestration of the liquid CO2 as well as additional utilization pathways.  We encourage the government to consider distribution hubs  outside of cities for liquid CO2 from where one can deliver the CO2 to utilizers or to sequestration hubs.  We also encourage the government to consider buildings as a valid carbon capture resource for sustainable CO2, especially because unlike the merchant market of commodity CO2,  we can verify capture levels in real time, calculate system efficiency, and trace the CO2 as recycled from a building.  There are many large state and federal buildings that could also benefit from this technology.  Our Building Carbon Capture systems work particularly well with energy management of the major equipment in the building - we optimize the energy use in buildings and partner to install energy management systems where needed as part of our projects to ensure maximum energy efficiency.
title: Comment from CarbonQuest

comment:
I’m deeply concerned about carbon capture, utilization, and sequestration (“CCUS”). CCUS is largely new and unproven technology, yet the federal government is preparing to spend billions of taxpayer dollars on this and other such schemes. President Biden and members of his administration have regularly and correctly named climate change as an existential threat to humanity, but investing in CCUS is a dangerous distraction from REAL climate solutions.

Capturing carbon dioxide is a very energy intensive process, and it allows for continued extraction and burning of coal, oil, and gas. Further, these operations have poisoned communities for decades, and capturing emissions at the final step of energy production does nothing to prevent the negative air, water, and health impacts associated with drilling and mining.

Developing CCUS at a large scale would also require thousands of miles of new pipelines to transport liquefied carbon dioxide. These pipelines pose a grave threat to public safety, as vapor clouds of carbon dioxide can easily spread for miles and lead to hallucinations, intoxication, asphyxiation, and death.

We need to transition our economy to 100% clean, renewable energy through rapid electrification, phasing out fossil fuels with the help of carbon taxes, and improved land management and restoration, keeping global warming at or below 1.5° C without utilizing CCUS.
